free.upa-2026-an1-1a:
Illness vs diseaseExplanatory modelsMedical pluralismCultural concepts of distress

Biomedicine treats health as a measurable bodily state; the WHO Constitution (1948) widened it to complete physical, mental and social well-being. Anthropologists show that what counts as sickness, what causes it and who should heal it are shaped by culture. Arthur Kleinman (Patients and Healers in the Context of Culture, 1980) called these shared ideas explanatory models, making health a cultural construct as much as a biological fact.

1. Sickness is defined by culture

  • Disease, illness, sickness: Leon Eisenberg (1977) and Kleinman separated disease, a malfunction diagnosed by the doctor, from illness, the sufferer's own experience; Allan Young (1982) added sickness, the social role a community grants to the sufferer.
  • Shifting boundaries: conditions such as obesity, alcoholism and ageing have been medicalised over time, so the line between normal and abnormal is drawn socially, not only by laboratories.
  • Three bodies: Nancy Scheper-Hughes and Margaret Lock (1987) showed that health is lived through the individual body, the social body and the body politic.

2. Causes and cures follow cultural logic

  • Etiologies: George Foster (1976) contrasted personalistic systems, where sickness is sent by a sorcerer, spirit or deity, with naturalistic ones based on balance of humours, hot and cold, or the doshas of Ayurveda. Among the Azande, E.E. Evans-Pritchard (1937) found that witchcraft explained why misfortune struck a particular person.
  • Culture-specific syndromes: dhat syndrome in South Asia, anxiety over loss of semen, and susto in Latin America make sense only within local ideas of the body; DSM-5 (2013) lists them as cultural concepts of distress.
  • Medical pluralism: Charles Leslie (Asian Medical Systems, 1976) showed patients moving between biomedicine, Ayurveda, Unani and folk healers; a Santal family may consult the ojha and the primary health centre for the same fever.

3. Why the construct matters

  • Health programmes: immunisation, institutional delivery or TB treatment succeed when they fit local explanatory models, which is why India's ASHA workers (2005) are recruited from the community and the AYUSH ministry (2014) recognises plural systems; the Abhay Bang expert committee on tribal health (2018) proposed trained local tribal youth (Aarogya Mitras) as a bridge.
  • Caution: critical medical anthropologists such as Paul Farmer warn that cultural explanations must not hide poverty and structural violence, which also make people ill.

Health is thus a biocultural reality: germs and genes are universal, but the meaning of suffering, the choice of healer and the idea of recovery are cultural. Culturally sensitive care is a practical necessity, not a courtesy.
free.upa-2026-an1-1b:
CanalizationCatch-up growthTarget-seeking growthGrowth centiles

Human growth follows a genetically set path that resists disturbance. C.H. Waddington (1942; The Strategy of the Genes, 1957) called this buffering canalization, picturing development as a ball rolling along valleys of an "epigenetic landscape". Catch-up growth, a term introduced by Prader, Tanner and von Harnack (1963), is its visible proof: once an illness or shortage ends, a child grows faster than normal and returns towards its original curve.

1. Canalization

  • Meaning: a developmental system that reaches the same end-point despite genetic or environmental disturbance; a growing child tends to stay in its own channel, a centile line on the growth chart.
  • Target-seeking growth: J.M. Tanner (1963) argued that a child behaves as if it had a target size set by its genotype and corrects deviations from it.
  • Evidence: healthy children keep close to the same height centile from early childhood to adolescence; in infancy many shift up or down to settle into the channel set by their genes rather than by the conditions in the womb.

2. Catch-up growth

  • Process: illness, hunger or hormone deficiency slows growth; when the cause is removed, height velocity rises well above the normal for that age until the deficit is made up, then slows again.
  • Examples: children treated for coeliac disease or hypothyroidism; most low-birth-weight babies, who catch up within the first two years; Romanian orphans adopted into English families in the early 1990s, who showed rapid gains in Michael Rutter's English and Romanian Adoptees study.
  • Limits: catch-up is incomplete when the insult is long or falls in a critical period, especially the first 1,000 days from conception to age two. David Barker's foetal-origins work linked rapid weight gain after poor foetal growth with later diabetes and heart disease.

3. Anthropological significance

  • Plasticity within limits: Franz Boas (1912) showed that children of immigrants in New York differed in body form from their parents, yet canalization explains why individuals rebound after short insults.
  • Public health: growth monitoring under ICDS and POSHAN Abhiyaan uses WHO growth standards to spot children who leave their channel; NFHS-6 (2023–24) found 29.3% of children under five stunted, down from 35.5% in NFHS-5, a sign of failed catch-up.

Canalization is the self-righting tendency of growth, and catch-up growth is how it shows itself. Both reveal growth as a bio-cultural process in which nutrition, health care and timing decide whether genetic potential is reached.
free.upa-2026-an2-1a:
Dravidian familyGondi and KurukhLanguage shiftLinguistic identity

The term Dravidian for India's second-largest language family was established by Robert Caldwell in his Comparative Grammar of the Dravidian or South-Indian Family of Languages (1856). Census 2011 lists 17 Dravidian languages spoken by about 19.6% of Indians. Besides the four great literary languages, the family includes many unwritten tribal languages spread across the central Indian highlands, the Nilgiris and the Rajmahal hills.

1. Branches and their tribal speakers

  • Four branches: Bhadriraju Krishnamurti (The Dravidian Languages, 2003) groups about two dozen languages into South, South-Central, Central and North Dravidian; apart from Tamil, Malayalam, Kannada, Telugu and Tulu, most of them are spoken by Scheduled Tribes.
  • Largest tribal languages: Gondi of the Gonds and Kurukh of the Oraons each have well over a million speakers (Census 2011); Kui and Kuvi of the Kondhs of Odisha come next.
  • Small communities: Toda, Kota, Kurumba, Irula and Koraga belong to small communities, the Toda and Kota only a few thousand strong and several of them PVTGs, so every lost speaker matters.
  • Historical clues: Oraon tradition, recorded by S.C. Roy (The Oraons of Chota Nagpur, 1915), recalls an earlier home at Rohtas, from where one branch went to the Rajmahal hills and another to Chotanagpur; the close kinship of Kurukh and Malto supports this shared origin of the Oraons and the Sauria Paharia.

2. Socio-linguistic features

  • Bilingualism and shift: most speakers also use a regional language; in many Oraon villages the lingua franca Sadri has displaced Kurukh, and many Gonds of Madhya Pradesh now speak Hindi dialects.
  • Language as identity: a shared tongue links a tribe across state borders, for example Kurukh speakers from Jharkhand to the tea gardens of Bengal and Assam, and has become a rallying point of ethnic assertion.

3. Revitalisation

  • Scripts and status: the Masaram and Gunjala Gondi scripts are now in Unicode, Tolong Siki is promoted for Kurukh, and Kurukh is an additional official language in Jharkhand and, since 2017, West Bengal; demands for Eighth Schedule status continue.
  • Mother-tongue schooling: Odisha's multilingual education programme in Kui, Kuvi and other tribal languages, and the NEP 2020 emphasis on the home language, aim to cut dropout among tribal children.

Dravidian tribal languages carry oral traditions and ecological knowledge; surveys such as the People's Linguistic Survey of India (from 2010) show that many are endangered, so schooling, media and official recognition decide their future.
free.upa-2026-an2-1b:
Clifford Jolly (1970)Gelada analogySmall-object feedingRamapithecus

The Seed Eaters Model was proposed by Clifford J. Jolly in The Seed-Eaters: A New Model of Hominid Differentiation Based on a Baboon Analogy (Man, 1970). Using the grassland-dwelling gelada baboon (Theropithecus gelada) as an analogy, Jolly argued that the first hominids split from the apes by adapting to small-object feeding (seeds, grass and roots) in open country, not by hunting. It was applied directly to Ramapithecus of the Indian Siwaliks.

1. The model

  • Analogy, not ancestry: geladas are not human ancestors, but they live in open, seasonal grassland; features they share with hominids, and not with forest apes, were read as convergent adaptations to the same diet.
  • Phase I, seed-eating: a ground-feeding primate picking up tiny, hard items while sitting or squatting would evolve small incisors, reduced canines, thick-enamelled grinding molars, a robust jaw, a precision grip and an upright trunk.
  • Phase II, meat-eating: hunting and tool use were added later in the line leading to Homo, while the robust australopithecines kept the seed-eating specialisation.
  • Against the hunting hypothesis: canine reduction was explained by the need for side-to-side grinding, not by tools replacing teeth as weapons, as Darwin (1871) and later Washburn had suggested.

2. Indian relevance: Ramapithecus

  • Siwalik fossil: Ramapithecus, named by G. Edward Lewis in 1934 from a Siwalik upper jaw, was treated by Elwyn Simons and David Pilbeam in the 1960s as the earliest hominid because of its thick enamel and small canines; Jolly's model gave it a dietary rationale.
  • Collapse of the claim: fuller Sivapithecus remains from the Potwar Plateau, especially a face described by Pilbeam in 1982, showed orangutan affinities; Ramapithecus was merged into Sivapithecus, and molecular dating (Sarich and Wilson, 1967) had already placed the human–ape split much later.

3. Evaluation

  • Weaknesses: geladas mainly eat grass blades rather than seeds; early hominins such as Ardipithecus ramidus (4.4 mya) lived in woodland, and dental microwear shows mixed diets, not a single grassland niche.
  • Partial support: carbon isotopes show that Paranthropus boisei ate mostly C4 grasses and sedges (Cerling and colleagues, 2011), echoing Jolly's view of the robust line.
  • Rival models: the gathering hypothesis of Tanner and Zihlman (1976) and Owen Lovejoy's food-sharing model (1981) offered other routes to bipedalism.

The Seed Eaters Model is now seen as heuristic: wrong about Ramapithecus, but lasting in its insight that diet and ecology shape teeth, hands and posture, an idea that isotope and microwear studies still test.
free.upa-2025-an1-1a:
Mendelian inheritancePolygenic traitsExtranuclear inheritanceGenomic imprinting

A Mendelian trait is controlled by a single gene and is transmitted according to the laws of segregation and independent assortment that Gregor Mendel derived from pea crosses (Experiments on Plant Hybridization, 1866), rediscovered in 1900. Non-Mendelian traits depart from these simple ratios because many genes, the environment, or inheritance outside the nuclear genes shape them.

1. Mendelian (monogenic) traits

  • Discrete phenotypes: individuals fall into clear classes (affected or unaffected), and matings give predictable ratios such as 3:1 or 1:1.
  • Modes of transmission: autosomal dominant (brachydactyly, which William Farabee in 1905 showed to be the first human trait inherited as a Mendelian dominant; Huntington disease), autosomal recessive (alkaptonuria, which Archibald Garrod tied to cousin marriage in 1902; albinism; sickle-cell anaemia) and X-linked recessive (haemophilia, red–green colour blindness).
  • Catalogue: Victor McKusick's Mendelian Inheritance in Man (1966), now the online OMIM database, lists thousands of such conditions.

2. Non-Mendelian traits

  • Polygenic and multifactorial: stature, skin colour, finger-ridge counts and blood pressure vary continuously along a bell curve; R.A. Fisher (1918) showed that many small Mendelian effects add up to such variation.
  • Departures from simple dominance: codominance (the AB and MN blood groups), multiple alleles (ABO), epistasis (the Bombay phenotype, in which an hh genotype hides ABO antigens, reported by Y.M. Bhende and colleagues in 1952) and incomplete penetrance.
  • Sex-influenced and sex-limited traits: pattern baldness is expressed far more often in men because of hormones, and some traits appear in one sex only, so ratios differ between sons and daughters.
  • Extranuclear (mitochondrial) inheritance: passed only through the mother, as in Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy; this maternal transmission underlies the "mitochondrial Eve" studies of human origins.
  • Imprinting and anticipation: the same chromosome 15 deletion causes Prader–Willi syndrome when inherited from the father and Angelman syndrome when inherited from the mother; repeat expansions (fragile X, myotonic dystrophy) worsen over generations.

3. Anthropological significance

  • Population history: Mendelian markers such as blood groups and haemoglobin variants trace gene flow and selection; the high frequency of the sickle-cell gene in tribal belts of central and southern India reflects balanced polymorphism against malaria.
  • Critique of race: skin colour and stature are polygenic and vary in clines, so they cannot sort humanity into discrete races.

The two classes are ends of a continuum: "simple" traits have modifier genes, and complex traits contain genes of large effect. Genomics and epigenetics now study both together to explain human variation and disease.
free.upa-2025-an1-1b:
PurumAsymmetric alliancePrescriptive marriageStructure and statistics

The Purum are a small Old Kuki, Tibeto-Burman-speaking community of the Manipur hills, numbering about 300 in four villages when T.C. Das described them in The Purums: An Old Kuki Tribe of Manipur (1945). Their rule of marrying into the mother's brother's group made them the classic test case of alliance theory, and one of the most re-analysed kinship systems in anthropology.

1. The kinship system

  • Descent: five exogamous patrilineal sibs (Marrim, Makan, Kheyang, Thao and Parpa), subdivided into lineages.
  • Marriage rule: matrilateral cross-cousin marriage: a man should take a wife from his mother's brother's lineage and must not take one from his father's sister's lineage.
  • Wife-givers and wife-takers: each lineage receives women from one set of lineages and gives them to another, so women move in one direction and the relation is never reversed.

2. Theoretical significance

  • Test of generalised exchange: Claude Lévi-Strauss (The Elementary Structures of Kinship, 1949) argued that matrilateral marriage links groups in a circle and builds wider solidarity than direct sister exchange. Rodney Needham's "A Structural Analysis of Purum Society" (American Anthropologist, 1958) used Das's data to show such a circulating connubium among Purum lineages.
  • Structure versus sentiment: George Homans and David Schneider (Marriage, Authority, and Final Causes, 1955) explained the matrilateral preference psychologically, by a boy's affection for his mother's brother in patrilineal societies. Needham's Structure and Sentiment (1962) replied that the rule follows from the logic of alliance between groups, not from individual feelings.
  • Prescription versus preference: Needham held that the Purum terminology itself defines a category of marriageable women, so marriage is prescribed, not merely preferred; Lévi-Strauss later played this distinction down (preface to the 1967 edition).
  • Model versus behaviour: Charles Ackerman ("Structure and Statistics: The Purum Case", 1964) tested Das's marriage records and found no clear avoidance of direct exchange. The debate sharpened the contrast between normative (mechanical) and statistical models.

3. Wider relevance

  • Similar one-way alliance among the Kachin (mayu–dama), analysed by Edmund Leach, points to a regional pattern in north-east India and Myanmar.
  • The Purum case shows the lasting value of detailed genealogies, which allow later scholars to test new theories.

A community of a few hundred people thus shaped a worldwide debate: it established alliance theory as a rival to descent theory and taught anthropologists to test elegant models against actual marriages.

SoanianPebble toolsSiwalik terracesMovius Line

The Soanian (or Sohanian) is a Lower Palaeolithic pebble-tool tradition named after the Soan, a tributary of the Indus on the Potwar plateau, now in Pakistan. It was defined by Helmut de Terra and T.T. Paterson of the Yale–Cambridge expedition of 1935, who in Studies on the Ice Age in India and Associated Human Cultures (1939) linked the tools to river terraces of a supposed Himalayan glacial sequence.

1. Distinctive features

  • Pebble technology: rounded quartzite pebbles from the Upper Siwalik boulder conglomerate were flaked to give a cutting edge, while the smooth cortex served as the grip.
  • Tool kit: unifacial choppers, bifacial chopping tools, discoids, scrapers and simple flakes; hand-axes and cleavers are rare or absent.
  • Phases: de Terra and Paterson separated an Early Soan of rolled pebble tools on the higher terrace from a Late Soan with more flakes, some from prepared cores, on a lower terrace; Acheulian hand-axes also turned up at Chauntra in the same valley.
  • Setting: open-air sites on terraces and fans of the Siwalik frontal zone.

2. Distribution in India

  • Sub-Himalayan belt: the Beas and Banganga valleys of Kangra (Guler, Dehra), described by B.B. Lal (1956); the Sirsa valley near Nalagarh and the Chandigarh–Pinjore area, explored by G.C. Mohapatra; the Jammu foothills.
  • Wider spread: choppers also occur within peninsular Acheulian assemblages, so pebble tools are not unique to the north.

3. Significance and re-evaluation

  • Movius Line: Hallam Movius (1948) grouped the Soanian with a "chopper–chopping tool" complex of East and South-East Asia, set against the hand-axe world of Africa and western Eurasia.
  • Dating revised: Robin Dennell and Helen Rendell's re-survey of the Potwar in the 1980s rejected the glacial-terrace scheme; many Soanian pieces are surface finds, and several assemblages are Middle or Late Pleistocene.
  • Facies, not a people: Soanian and Acheulian tools are now found together in the Siwalik frontal zone, so many scholars treat the Soanian as a raw-material or activity facies rather than a separate, older culture.
  • Early claims: artefacts at Riwat (Pakistan, about 2 mya) and cut-marked bones at Masol near Chandigarh (about 2.6 mya, reported in 2016) keep the question of the first toolmakers open, but both claims are contested.

The Soanian is best understood as a pebble-tool facies of the Lower Palaeolithic in the Siwalik zone. It shaped the early history of Indian prehistory and the Movius debate, but its age and its separateness from the Acheulian still need firm dating.
free.upa-2025-an2-1b:
Dominant casteFactionalismVote bankPoliticisation of caste

M.N. Srinivas first used the idea of the dominant caste in "The Social System of a Mysore Village" (1955) and developed it in "The Dominant Caste in Rampura" (American Anthropologist, 1959). Caste domination, internal factionalism and political power form a chain: the dominant caste controls the village, its rival factions compete for that control, and electoral democracy has carried the contest to district and state politics.

1. Caste domination

  • Attributes: a caste dominates when it is numerically strong, owns much of the arable land, wields political power and holds a fairly high ritual rank; Srinivas later added Western education, government jobs and urban income.
  • Examples: Okkaligas in Rampura and Lingayats in Karnataka, Reddis and Kammas in Andhra, Jats in Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, Marathas in Maharashtra and Patidars in Gujarat.
  • Exercise of power: it settles disputes, sets local norms and controls patronage, as Jat khap panchayats do.

2. Factionalism

  • Nature: Ralph Nicholas (1965) described factions as political conflict groups that are not corporate; a leader recruits followers through kinship, patronage, debt or economic dependence.
  • Inside the dominant caste: Srinivas found factionalism endemic within the dominant caste. Rival leaders belong to it and draw followers vertically from lower castes, so factions cut across caste lines. Oscar Lewis (Village Life in Northern India, 1958) found Jat factions in a village near Delhi organised along lineage lines.
  • Triggers: land disputes, panchayat polls, schemes and party rivalry.

3. Political power

  • Vote bank: Srinivas coined the term in 1955 for the bloc of votes a patron could deliver; factions became the local units of party politics, as Paul Brass showed for the Congress in Uttar Pradesh (1965).
  • Politicisation of caste: Rajni Kothari (Caste in Indian Politics, 1970) argued that caste was organised for politics while politics drew on caste loyalties; the Rudolphs (1967) saw caste associations as vehicles of democratic participation.
  • Shifting power: André Béteille (Caste, Class and Power, 1965) showed power in Sripuram passing from Brahmin landlords to non-Brahmin politicians, separating power from ritual rank.
  • Challenges: reserved seats in panchayats (73rd Amendment, 1992) and assertion by Dalits and backward classes now contest old dominance, sometimes provoking violent backlash.
  • Critique: later village studies found power resting with a few lineages or leaders rather than the whole caste, and A.C. Mayer (1958) showed that dominance often works across a region rather than within one village.

Domination, faction and power form a single cycle in rural India. Democratic decentralisation has widened access to office, but it has also turned caste into a resource for electoral mobilisation.
free.upa-2024-an1-1a:
CultureLearned and sharedSymbolicIntegrated and dynamic

Culture is the design for living that a people learn and share. E.B. Tylor (Primitive Culture, 1871) gave the classic definition: "that complex whole which includes knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom, and any other capabilities and habits acquired by man as a member of society." Clifford Geertz (The Interpretation of Cultures, 1973) stressed its web of meanings. Both point to attributes found in every culture.

1. Attributes that define culture

  • Learned, not inherited: culture is acquired after birth through enculturation (M.J. Herskovits's term). An infant adopted across continents grows up with the speech, food habits and manners of the adoptive family, not of its biological parents.
  • Shared: culture belongs to a group, so members can predict one another's conduct. Ralph Linton (The Study of Man, 1936) showed that sharing is uneven: universals are held by all adults, specialties by particular groups (a potter caste, a priest), alternatives by a few.
  • Symbolic: meanings are fixed by convention, not by nature. Leslie White (The Science of Culture, 1949) treated the symbol as the basis of all culture; a mangalsutra, a national flag or a Toda sacred buffalo carries meaning only for those who share the code.
  • Transmitted and cumulative: language and writing store knowledge beyond any one lifetime; A.L. Kroeber called this level "superorganic" (1917).

2. Attributes that explain how culture works

  • Integrated: parts fit into a whole. Among the Todas of the Nilgiris (W.H.R. Rivers, 1906), buffalo herding links the economy, dairy temples, priesthood and kinship.
  • Adaptive: culture is the main human means of coping with environments, from Inuit snow houses to the stepwells and kunds of arid Rajasthan.
  • Dynamic: it changes through invention, diffusion and acculturation; W.F. Ogburn (Social Change, 1922) called the delay of beliefs and norms behind technology "cultural lag".

3. Universal yet particular

  • Universal: G.P. Murdock's "common denominator of cultures" (1945) lists family, language, religion and rules of property found everywhere.
  • Particular: each culture combines these differently, so it must be judged on its own terms (Boas's cultural relativism); Khasi inheritance through the youngest daughter differs sharply from the patrilineal norms of their neighbours.
  • Human in degree: chimpanzees at Gombe fish for termites with twigs (Jane Goodall), but only humans build cumulative, symbol-based culture.

These attributes make culture humanity's extra-somatic inheritance. They also warn against ranking cultures, which is why cultural relativism guides fieldwork and policy for tribal communities today.

MeluhhaLothalDilmun and MaganPersian Gulf seals

The Harappan (Indus) Civilization (mature phase c. 2600–1900 BCE) traded by sea with the Persian Gulf and Mesopotamia. Cuneiform texts call a distant eastern land Meluhha, widely identified with the Indus region and Gujarat coast, whose ships moored at Akkad in the reign of Sargon (c. 2334–2279 BCE). Archaeology from Gujarat to Oman and Iraq confirms this exchange.

1. Evidence of maritime trade

  • Ports and coastal sites: Lothal on the Gulf of Khambhat (excavated by S.R. Rao, 1955–62) had a large brick-lined basin read as a dockyard, a warehouse and bead workshops. Sutkagen-dor and Sotka-koh on the Makran coast, Balakot, Kuntasi and Dholavira were other coastal or near-coastal nodes.
  • Boats: a seal from Mohenjo-daro depicts a flat-bottomed boat with a central cabin, and Lothal yielded a terracotta boat model and stone anchors.
  • Harappan goods abroad: etched carnelian beads in the royal cemetery at Ur and at Kish; Indus seals and cubical chert weights in Mesopotamia and the Gulf; black-slipped Harappan storage jars at Ras al-Jinz and other sites in Oman.
  • Foreign objects at home: a round "Persian Gulf" type seal at Lothal.
  • Texts: a cylinder seal of Shu-ilishu names him an interpreter of the Meluhhan language, and later Ur III texts mention a "Meluhha village" near Lagash, pointing to resident traders.

2. Routes and goods

  • Coastal voyaging: ships followed the Makran coast to Magan (Oman) and Dilmun (Bahrain and Failaka), which became middlemen for Mesopotamia.
  • Exports: carnelian and other beads, ivory, shell objects, timber and gold.
  • Imports: copper from Oman by sea; lapis lazuli from Badakhshan (through the Harappan outpost of Shortughai), tin and silver came mainly overland, and some lapis was shipped on to Mesopotamia.

3. Significance and debates

  • Economic organisation: a single weight standard, seals for marking consignments and craft centres such as the shell-working sites of Nageshwar and Gola Dhoro point to organised merchant networks.
  • Debates: Lawrence Leshnik (1968) argued that the Lothal basin was a reservoir, not a dock; overseas trade was small compared with internal exchange; and references to Meluhha fade after c. 1900 BCE as Indus cities declined.

Sea trade shows the Harappans as an early Indian Ocean people whose seals, weights and beads crossed the Arabian Sea. It is a classic case of culture contact through commerce, and anticipates the later monsoon trade of the region.
free.upa-2024-an2-1a:
DigitisationJAM trinityDigital divideTechnoscapes

Digitisation of the rural economy is the shift of village credit, payments, markets, land records and welfare delivery onto digital platforms. Since Digital India (2015) and the JAM trinity (Jan Dhan accounts, Aadhaar and mobile phones), the Indian village has entered what Arjun Appadurai (1990) called global technoscapes, which are reshaping old patron–client ties and creating new divides.

1. Instruments of digitisation

  • Money and welfare: Jan Dhan accounts (2014), Aadhaar-based Direct Benefit Transfer and UPI (2016) now carry MGNREGA wages, pensions and PM-KISAN instalments (₹6,000 a year since 2019) straight to rural households.
  • Markets and farming: e-NAM (2016) links agricultural mandis online, and the Digital Agriculture Mission (2024) is building an Agri Stack of farmer IDs and digital crop surveys.
  • Land and governance: SVAMITVA (2020) maps village house sites by drone and gives owners property cards usable as collateral; Common Service Centres and BharatNet take e-governance to gram panchayats.

2. Changes in village society and economy

  • Fewer middlemen: direct transfers reduce leakages and weaken the hold of the moneylender, ration dealer and trader; Robin Jeffrey and Assa Doron's Cell Phone Nation (2013) shows how the mobile phone gave farmers, fishers and small traders price information and new bargaining power.
  • New roles for women: women of self-help groups work as banking correspondents and, under the Namo Drone Didi scheme (2023), as drone operators for spraying crops, entering public economic roles once closed to them.
  • Translocal households: instant transfers tie migrant workers in cities to families in the village, so the village economy now extends far beyond its boundary.

3. Concerns from an anthropological view

  • Digital divide: women who had ever used the internet rose from 33% in NFHS-5 (2019–21) to 64% in NFHS-6 (2023–24), yet over a third had never gone online; older, poorer and remote Adivasi households lag further behind.
  • Exclusion errors: failed biometric authentication or unlinked records can cut off rations and wages; the death of eleven-year-old Santoshi Kumari in Simdega, Jharkhand (2017), after her family's ration card was cancelled for want of Aadhaar linking, became a symbol of this risk.
  • New dependencies: kiosk operators and agents emerge as fresh intermediaries, while the collection of personal data raises issues of privacy and surveillance.

Digitisation is turning the village as a social system from a face-to-face, patron-based economy into a networked one. Its gains will be inclusive only if digital literacy (PMGDISHA), local-language platforms and offline grievance options reach women, the elderly and remote Adivasi hamlets.

State formationChiefdom to stateCircumscription theoryRajput myth

A state society has a centralised government that claims, in Max Weber's sense, a monopoly of legitimate force over a territory, supported by taxation, a bureaucracy, law and class stratification. In Elman Service's sequence of band, tribe, chiefdom and state (Primitive Social Organization, 1962) and Morton Fried's sequence of egalitarian, rank, stratified and state societies (1967), the state is the most complex form of political organisation.

1. Theories of the origin of the state

  • Integrative theories: Karl Wittfogel (Oriental Despotism, 1957) linked early states to the management of large irrigation works; others stress the control of long-distance trade and the redistribution of surplus.
  • Conflict theories: Friedrich Engels (The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State, 1884) saw the state as the instrument of a propertied class; Robert Carneiro (1970) argued that population growth in circumscribed land, such as the narrow coastal valleys of Peru, led to warfare, conquest and centralised rule.
  • Urban revolution: V. Gordon Childe (1950) tied the state to food surplus, full-time specialists, writing and monumental building in the first cities.

2. How archaeology recognises a state

  • Settlement hierarchy: three or more tiers of settlement (capital, towns, villages) point to administrative control, as Henry Wright and Gregory Johnson (1975) argued for early south-western Iran.
  • Material markers: palaces, temples, standard weights, seals, writing, fortifications and differences in burial wealth reveal central authority and inequality.

3. State formation in India

  • Harappan civilisation: planned cities, uniform weights and seals suggest strong authority, yet the lack of palaces and royal tombs led Gregory Possehl to describe a complex society without a clear state, while others speak of city-states.
  • Ganga valley: Romila Thapar's From Lineage to State (1984) traces how iron-age surplus and ranked clans turned gana-sanghas into monarchies, leading to the Mahajanapadas (c. 6th century BCE) and the rise of Magadha.
  • Tribal states: Surajit Sinha (1962) showed how chiefs in tribal central India, such as those of the Bhumij, claimed Rajput descent to legitimise kingship; the Nagvanshis of Chotanagpur and the Ahom kingdom of Assam are other cases of tribal state formation.

The state thus arose from multiple causes working together: surplus, population pressure, war, trade and ritual legitimation. Indian evidence, from Harappa to the kingdoms of Chotanagpur, also explains present-day tribe–state relations.
free.upa-2023-an1-1a:
Social anthropologyCultural anthropologyHolism and fieldworkApplied relevance

Social-cultural anthropology studies how people live together and make sense of their world: their institutions, beliefs and everyday practices. The British tradition of social anthropology (A.R. Radcliffe-Brown, E.E. Evans-Pritchard) focused on social structure, while American cultural anthropology (Franz Boas, A.L. Kroeber) focused on culture, which E.B. Tylor (Primitive Culture, 1871) described as the complex whole that humans acquire as members of society. Today the two are treated as one field.

1. Scope

  • Social institutions: kinship, marriage, family, economy, polity, law and religion are studied as linked parts of one whole (holism); Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922) traced how the Kula exchange tied Trobriand trade, magic and politics together.
  • Culture and the individual: socialisation, personality and values, from Margaret Mead's Coming of Age in Samoa (1928) to present-day studies of emotion, gender and identity.
  • Change and continuity: diffusion, acculturation, modernisation and globalisation; M.N. Srinivas's Sanskritisation and S.C. Dube's Indian Village (1955) traced change in Indian rural life.
  • Distinct method: long fieldwork, participant observation, the genealogical method and cross-cultural comparison give an insider (emic) view along with the observer's (etic) view.
  • Widening field: medical, urban, legal, environmental, development, visual and digital anthropology now study cities, firms, hospitals and online communities, not only "simple" societies.

2. Relevance

  • Understanding diversity: cultural relativism counters ethnocentrism and racism, vital in a plural society; the Anthropological Survey of India's People of India project (led by K.S. Singh) documented 4,635 communities.
  • Tribal policy and development: Verrier Elwin's advice shaped Nehru's tribal Panchsheel; anthropologists contribute to social impact assessment, resettlement of displaced people and the working of the Forest Rights Act, 2006.
  • Health: ethnography of burial customs helped contain the Ebola epidemic in West Africa (2014–16) and explains vaccine hesitancy; in India it guides maternal-health and sickle-cell programmes in tribal areas.
  • Governance and conflict: knowledge of ethnic identity, customary law and village institutions helps peace-building in the Northeast and the working of PESA, 1996.
  • Economy and technology: ethnographic methods are now used in market research, user-experience design and corporate studies.

Social-cultural anthropology has moved from describing "other" cultures to understanding all societies, including our own. Its holistic, people-centred lens makes it essential for inclusive development and culturally sensitive public policy.
free.upa-2023-an1-1b:
Iron AgePainted Grey WareMegalithic cultureSecond urbanisation

The Iron Age begins when smelted iron replaces bronze and stone as the main material for tools and weapons. Iron-working spread from Anatolia and the Near East (widely after about 1200 BCE) to Europe (Hallstatt and La Tène cultures) and Africa (Nok, Nigeria). In India iron appears in the Painted Grey Ware (PGW) culture of the Ganga–Yamuna doab and in the Megalithic burials of the Deccan and the south, with dates of about 1800–1000 BCE at sites such as Malhar (Uttar Pradesh) and Hallur (Karnataka).

1. Economic impact

  • Forest clearance and farming: iron axes, sickles and ploughshares opened the heavy, forested soils of the middle Ganga plain; D.D. Kosambi and later R.S. Sharma (Material Culture and Social Formations in Ancient India, 1983) linked this to wet-rice cultivation and a food surplus.
  • Craft specialisation: smiths became a distinct group; the craft survives among the Lohar and among the Agaria and Asur iron-smelting communities (Verrier Elwin, The Agaria, 1942).
  • Trade and money: surplus supported long-distance trade, punch-marked coins and the fine Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW, c. 700–200 BCE).

2. Social and political impact

  • Second urbanisation: towns such as Rajagriha, Kaushambi and Shravasti and the sixteen Mahajanapadas (6th century BCE) rose on this surplus, with taxation and standing armies; Magadha's rise has been linked to its access to iron ore.
  • Cheaper metal, wider use: V. Gordon Childe (What Happened in History, 1942) argued that cheap, abundant iron put tools and weapons in the hands of ordinary farmers and soldiers.
  • Stratification: control over land, cattle and metal deepened inequality between chiefs, warriors, peasants and artisans.

3. Ideological and cultural impact

  • Megalithic burials at Brahmagiri, Junapani and Adichanallur, with iron weapons, horse fittings and Black-and-Red Ware, suggest chiefdoms, ancestor cults and belief in an afterlife.
  • New religious ideas: Buddhism and Jainism, which rejected costly animal sacrifice, suited a peasant economy that needed its cattle (R.S. Sharma).
  • Living megalithic tradition: the Khasi, Jaintia, Naga and Munda still raise memorial stones, linking Iron Age burials to living tribal belief.

4. Debate

  • A. Ghosh and others argued that early iron was too scarce to clear forests and that fire did much of the work. Tamil Nadu's 2025 report dating iron at Sivagalai to about 3345 BCE, like the early Malhar dates, remains disputed.

The Iron Age was thus a technological and social turning point: it laid the material base for early states, cities and new faiths, working together with rice farming, trade and political ambition.
free.upa-2023-an2-1a:
Material cultureArchaeological recordFormation processesEthnoarchaeology

Material culture is the physical world that people make, use and throw away: tools, pots, houses, ornaments, graves and altered landscapes. Archaeology studies past societies almost entirely through such remains, so the two are inseparable. Because objects do not speak, archaeologists turn to ethnoarchaeology, the study of material culture among living communities, to read behaviour from things.

1. Material culture as archaeological evidence

  • Artefacts, ecofacts and features: portable objects (handaxes, microliths, beads), organic remains (seeds, animal bones) and fixed traces (hearths, post-holes, burials) together make up the archaeological record.
  • Cultures as assemblages: V. Gordon Childe (The Danube in Prehistory, 1929) treated an archaeological culture as a recurring set of pottery, tools, house forms and burial rites; Indian sequences such as Ochre Coloured Pottery followed by Painted Grey Ware are built in this way.
  • Objects carry meaning: Ian Hodder (Symbols in Action, 1982), working in Kenya's Baringo district, showed that people use dress, ornaments and pottery to mark group identity, so material culture is active, not a passive mirror.

2. From objects to behaviour

  • Formation processes: Michael Schiffer (Behavioral Archeology, 1976) separated the living "systemic context" from the "archaeological context"; discard, reuse, decay and later disturbance decide what survives.
  • Middle-range theory: Lewis Binford (Nunamiut Ethnoarchaeology, 1978) recorded how Nunamiut caribou hunters of Alaska butchered, stored and discarded bones, giving rules for reading ancient bone scatters.
  • Analogy: direct historical analogy where living people descend from the excavated ones, and general comparative analogy between societies in similar environments.

3. Indian applications

  • Megalithic survivals: Khasi memorial stones (upright "male" and flat "female" slabs), Munda burial slabs (sasandiri) and Maria Gond memorial pillars help interpret the Iron Age megaliths of the peninsula.
  • Crafts: Carol Kramer's Pottery in Rajasthan (1997) studied potters in two cities, showing how caste, workshops and markets shape the making and spread of pots, a guide for reading ancient pottery.
  • Harappan analogies: from John Marshall onward, excavators read terracotta bullock carts, ploughs and bangles through their present-day village equivalents.
  • Prehistoric landscapes: K. Paddayya used present-day seasonal patterns of water, plants and game in the Hunsgi–Baichbal valleys (Karnataka) to model Acheulian settlement.

4. Limits

  • Living people are not fossils: steel and plastic vessels, markets and migration have transformed crafts, so analogies need caution, and fieldwork needs informed consent.

Material culture is the bridge between present and past; joined with ethnoarchaeology and scientific dating, it lets archaeology move from describing objects to explaining human behaviour.
free.upa-2023-an2-1b:
PurusharthaAshramaDharmaMoksha

In the classical Hindu scheme, Purushartha names the four legitimate aims of life (dharma, artha, kama and moksha), while Ashrama divides the ideal life of a twice-born man into four stages. P.H. Prabhu (Hindu Social Organization, 1954) showed that the two were designed together: the stages are the social settings in which the aims are pursued in turn, always under the guidance of dharma.

1. Each stage emphasises different aims

  • Brahmacharya (student): begins with upanayana; celibacy, study and obedience to the guru teach dharma and prepare the youth for later duties.
  • Grihastha (householder): begins with marriage (vivaha); artha (wealth) and kama (desire and family life) are pursued within dharma, the debts (rinas) to gods, sages and ancestors are repaid, and the Dharmashastras praise this stage as the support of all the others.
  • Vanaprastha (forest dweller): when grandchildren arrive, worldly pursuits are reduced and dharma is turned towards preparing for liberation.
  • Sannyasa (renouncer): all ties are given up in search of moksha, release from the cycle of birth and rebirth.

2. Principles that join the two

  • Dharma as regulator: artha and kama are valid only when bounded by dharma; Kautilya's Arthashastra and Vatsyayana's Kamasutra treat these aims as sciences, yet within a moral order.
  • Pravritti and nivritti: the first two stages engage with the world and the last two withdraw from it, balancing material and spiritual life across a lifetime.
  • Links with samskara and karma: life-cycle rites mark entry into each stage, and right action in each stage shapes the next birth.

3. Anthropological appraisal

  • An ideal, not a universal practice: the Dharmashastras addressed the scheme to twice-born men; women and Shudras were largely outside upanayana, and Manu treats marriage as a woman's equivalent of initiation.
  • Historical change: Patrick Olivelle (The Asrama System, 1993) shows that the ashramas were first alternative lifelong paths and only later became a fixed sequence.
  • Householder and renouncer: Louis Dumont (1960) contrasted the man-in-the-world with the renouncer as an individual outside society, while T.N. Madan (Non-renunciation, 1987) found Kashmiri Pandits valuing detachment within household life.

Few follow the stages literally today, yet the ideal survives in retirement, pilgrimage and service to family, and its lesson, a balance of material and spiritual aims, remains relevant.
